item.title: Three LLM inflection points in twelve months
item.description: I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months. Here's the video of the talk. In this post I'm going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply. Coding agents in November 2025 Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5 . With hindsight, this was a consequential model. In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said: Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach. This held up. Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025. Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn't been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn't feel reliable enough - I had to correct it often enough that it didn't feel like a clear accelerant. The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right . It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself. Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks. The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work. Fable class models in June/July We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release , due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them. In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5 - a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work. After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn't get it back until July 1st. For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as Fable class models . My definition of these: In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive , after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug. A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago. I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm. Give it a goal, give it the right tools, and watch it cook. I'd currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as "cheap Fable"). GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well. These now represent the baseline for what I expect from a frontier model. 3D modeling and game development in September/October Something interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got really good at 3D modeling. Set them up with Blender or ask them to write Three.js code and they'll produce credible models of almost anything you ask for. I first noticed this with Claude Fable 5, but it really kicked into gear with Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and most recently the Gemini 4 family. Here's Gemini 4 Neon's attempt at "Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data", for example. 3D spatial awareness is crucial if you want to use vision LLMs for robotics. I don't know if 3D modeling capabilities are a side-effect of the labs focusing on that or vice-versa. Back in August I experimented with having Fable 5 build me a raccoon heist game . It had 3D graphics, looked like a game, and played really poorly. GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra did a much better job but the game itself was still pretty dull after the first 90 seconds of play. I was somewhat relieved that designing a game that was fun appeared to remain a uniquely human pursuit. I even used that in a talk in September to reassure people that us humans still had a role to play! Then, I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 "This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun." And it worked . My Command & Conquer-style RTS went from boring to deeply entertaining overnight, after Opus spent 12 hours playtesting new features and rebalancing the gameplay. Opus 5.5 was the first model I'd used that appeared to understand fun. I've since worked on several little game projects where prompts like "Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful" produced results that kept me engaged for significant amounts of time. Opus 5.5 came out on September 22nd, 2026. I've been to two different conferences since then where people showed me game projects they'd been working on that really did feel like proper, worthwhile games. The indie games scene has descended into a full-blown culture war over AI-assisted programming. A lot of people are calling GTA VI the last pre-generative AI blockbuster . It feels like another inflection point to me. Is Fable 5.2 an inflection point too? I'm still trying to decide if Fable 5.2 represents a new inflection point, or just another incremental improvement. I'm getting so much done with that model right now! It seems to have taste that almost exactly matches my own. I have been burning through all sorts of gnarly problems that I've been thinking about (or procrastinating on) for several years now. The release notes for Datasette 1.0a42 , 1.0a43 , and 1.0a44 - plus LLM 0.37 , 0.37.1 , 0.37.2 , 0.37.3 , and 0.38 - all in the last three weeks , represent a flood of fixes, features and improvements. If this does represent an inflection point, the key feature seems to be that if you can imagine and then clearly describe a piece of software, Fable can build it . That's a wild thing to say, but it matches my experience over the past few weeks. Software development has transformed beyond recognition in the last year. I don't think I'll ever go back to typing most of my code by hand. item.title: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery
item.description: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries: With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library . It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians. Here's the digitized sketchbook . Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work. Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue ? Mark thinks it will be mild: But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians, on the other hand, constantly reinterpret the past in light of an evolving present; we don’t chase a single universal truth. We also (in the ideal at least) write books and articles that are closer to works of philosophy and literature than they are to scientific tracts. Humanity is thus something of a requirement for the production of historical literature. Tags: history , ai , generative-ai , llms , ai-assisted-search , deep-blue , gpt-6-astra

item.title: We Get the Infrastructure We Pay For
item.description: This essay originally appeared as part of a round table in The Free Press entitled "Is America’s Infrastructure Under Attack?" Microsoft, the FAA, banks, United Airlines, the NSA—it's been a really bad week in cyberspace. But, amazing as it might seem, these are not related. As far as we know, they're not the result of cyberattacks. They're not even related to AI. (Well, that's mostly true. The NSA will probably never tell us what went wrong.) It's really just a series of unfortunate coincidences. Our computerized infrastructure is vulnerable and fragile. Much of it is old, and has been incrementally patched and upgraded. A surprising amount of it is maintained by hobbyists, without any recompense. And more and more of it is centralized: the same systems affecting many different aspects of our lives and society. In many cases, it just barely works. And when it fails, it tends to fail badly...

item.title: CISA Adds Three Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
item.description: CISA has added three new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-131914 Idunno AntiCsrf Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability  CVE-2026-132165 Drupal Core Remote Code Execution Vulnerability  CVE-2026-132224 Optimizely Web Experimentation External Control of Critical State Data Vulnerability  These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

item.title: Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series
item.description: View CSAF Summary Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code with webserver privileges. The following versions of Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series are affected: AK-SM8xxA CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 9.8 Danfoss AK-SM8xxA 1 Vulnerability Stack-based Buffer Overflow Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Commercial Facilities Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Denmark Vulnerabilities CVE-2026-129713 A stack-based buffer overflow in an unauthenticated CGI handler of the Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series controller allows remote attackers to send specially crafted HTTP/S POST requests, leading to memory corruption, webserver restart and hypothetically potential arbitrary code execution with webserver privileges. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability. Read More 1 Affected Product Danfoss AK-SM8xxA Product Status: known_affected Remediations Mitigation This vulnerability will be addressed in an upcoming Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series software release (version 5.5.x). In addition, Danfoss will remove the ability for users to disable Strict Mode in future software releases. Mitigation Until a software update is available, Danfoss recommends the following mitigations: * Follow the guidance provided in the product documentation and do not expose devices directly to the Internet or assign them public IP addresses. * Restrict remote access to affected devices by using a secure VPN or other protected network architecture. * Configure all affected devices to operate in Strict Mode, which provides enhanced security protections. * Use strong, unique passwords for all user accounts and administrative access. * For additional security recommendations and best practices see the Danfoss AK-SM 800 security guidance page: https://www.danfoss.com/en/service-and-support/downloads/dcs/adap-kool-software/ak-sm-800a/#tab-overview Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-121 Stack-based Buffer Overflow CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 9.8 CRITICAL CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H 4.0 9.3 CRITICAL CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N View CVE Details Acknowledgments Carlo Meijer of Midnight Blue reported CVE-2026-129713 to CISA. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet . Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics . Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies . CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets . Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies . Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks: Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages. Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams. Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks. No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time. item.title: As Corporate Bond Markets Grow, Is Bank Lending Shrinking?
item.description: The size of global corporate bond markets has increased dramatically over the past three decades. As of the end of 2024, nonfinancial corporate bonds issued by U.S. firms accounted for 29 percent of U.S. GDP. In other advanced economies, though bond markets remain smaller than in the U.S., corporate bonds were on average 11 percent of GDP in the same year. This growth is usually read as a shift from bank to market finance. But the ratio of bonds to GDP can rise either because firms take more debt in general, or because firms shift the composition of their debt toward bonds. In this post, we document growth in bonds to GDP for both the U.S. and other advanced economies, and argue that the sources of that growth are different across countries and have changed over time.

item.title: Built for trust and control: Powering the next wave of AI agents across Google Workspace and Google Cloud
item.description: For over 20 years, we have protected 4 billion users and 13 million organizations in Workspace, and critical enterprise and government systems on Google Cloud. From personal and financial records to board materials, regulated workloads, applications, and AI models, those safeguards protect what matters most. Blocking >99.9% of spam, phishing, and malware, alongside encryption and data residency, follows one principle: your data is yours, and you should always know and decide who can access it. That trust has powered one of the world’s largest developer ecosystems. Workspace APIs now handle more than 2.8 trillion calls a month, and public Google Drive API traffic alone is more than two-and-a-half times the volume of 2022. More than 18 billion reads from Drive each day come from API callers. Traditional REST APIs were built for human-paced apps where a valid OAuth token implied user intent. As AI agents shift from reading information to acting autonomously at machine speed across email, documents, datasets, and cloud infrastructure, a valid token is no longer enough. Policy checks, data boundaries, and human confirmation have to live in the request path. Today, Workspace MCP servers and the Workspace CLI are generally available alongside Google Cloud Agent Gateway and unified protections across Workspace and Google Cloud. Builders get modern, agent-ready interfaces, and organizations get the visibility and control to adopt AI agents with confidence. Purpose-built interfaces: Workspace MCP servers, Workspace CLI, and Cloud Agent Gateway To help developers build reliable agents faster without forcing security teams to compromise, we are bringing agent-native interfaces to Workspace and Google Cloud: Workspace MCP servers : Now generally available, dedicated remote servers for Gmail, Google Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Chat, and Tasks. Builders get one standard interface with built-in permission and DLP checks, and native human-in-the-loop (HITL) confirmations for sensitive actions. They also reject non-agent OAuth clients and work with Model Armor, Google Cloud’s prompt-injection screening service. Workspace CLI : Now generally available for local agents, terminal workflows, and automation, providing structured JSON outputs and scoped OAuth sign-in across Workspace services. Google Cloud Agent Gateway : A protocol-native gateway for LLM, MCP, and Agent2Agent (A2A) traffic on Google Cloud. It verifies Agent Identities against Agent Registry, enforces IAM policies and default-deny outbound rules, and screens requests with Model Armor. Together, these interfaces give AI agents open, protocol-native paths built on standards like MCP and A2A. Permissions, confirmations, prompt screening, and audit logging happen automatically, while traditional apps continue to run on existing REST APIs. Consistent controls across every agent workflow Those interfaces sit on a unified security model across Workspace and Google Cloud, with core controls shipping today: Policy checks on every request: Under our new Workspace AI Tools Addendum , AI agents must use Workspace MCP servers or the Workspace CLI rather than existing REST APIs. Technical enforcement begins on February 1, 2027, giving builders time to transition. Every call is checked against your organization’s Workspace permissions, DLP rules, and classification labels. On Google Cloud, Agent Gateway enforces IAM and default-deny outbound rules at the protocol layer and routes custom checks through Service Extensions to Identity-Aware Proxy, your own policy engine, or third-party security tools. Separate agent identities and limits: Admins and users need to tell an AI agent apart from a traditional app or a person, and cap what it can do. Agents connecting to Workspace must use dedicated OAuth client IDs , paired with least-privilege scopes, time-limited approvals (coming soon), and usage quotas (billing begins on April 1, 2027). On Google Cloud, agents receive their own Agent Identity in Agent Registry with no shared or long-lived keys, bounded by IAM policies and organization, folder, and project quotas. Those identities can also carry user-delegated authorization into Workspace when accessing mail or files. People stay in charge of high-impact actions: Routine work like creating drafts or summarizing documents runs autonomously, while critical changes require a person to sign off. In Workspace, MCP servers and the CLI enforce explicit user confirmation before agents send email, change Drive sharing permissions, or make bulk edits. On Google Cloud, policy can require multi-factor authentication or human approval before reading sensitive Cloud Storage buckets, changing IAM permissions, or modifying production infrastructure. Clear visibility and revocation: A one-time consent screen is not enough when agents run continuously. Workspace administrators can view, audit, and revoke AI agents in the admin console , and users will soon be able to view agent activity and revoke access to their emails and files. On Google Cloud, Security Command Center, Agent Observability, Cloud Audit Logs, and Wiz surface unusual behavior. Revoking a Cloud Agent Identity or OAuth grant stops access immediately. Boundaries for your most sensitive data: Coming soon in Workspace, AI access restrictions extend Workspace DLP and client-side encryption protections to agents. This will allow admins and users to block agents from accessing messages in Gmail and specific files and folders in Drive. On Google Cloud, VPC Service Controls, Principal Access Boundaries, and Context-Aware Access keep sensitive data inside designated perimeters and verified devices. Strict rules on your data afterward: Our new Workspace AI Tools Addendum sets clear boundaries for AI tools using Workspace APIs. It does not allow permanent raw storage, model training, extended retention of derived data, or API scraping. Derived and user data are removed within a defined window and when a user disconnects. On Google Cloud, Sensitive Data Protection masks sensitive fields before data leaves, and customer-managed or external encryption keys let you cut off access to Cloud agent memory stores immediately. Getting started Workspace developers: Start building with the Workspace MCP and CLI configuration guide , implement user confirmations via MCP and prompt-injection protection such as Model Armor, and review the Workspace AI Tools Addendum . Workspace administrators: Review connected apps and agents, configure DLP policies for your users, and monitor OAuth activity logs in the admin console . Google Cloud customers: Register Agent Identities in Agent Registry, place Agent Gateway and Model Armor in front of agents and MCP servers, configure MFA or human approval for sensitive actions, and review IAM, VPC Service Controls, and quota limits. With Workspace MCP servers and the Workspace CLI generally available alongside Google Cloud’s agent protections, developers have an open, modern platform to build on. Organizations get the visibility and control to scale AI agents with confidence.

item.title: Enabling zero trust: ALLEN’s move to Chrome Enterprise Premium
item.description: Editor’s note: Founded in 1988 in Kota, Rajasthan, ALLEN is one of India’s leading coaching institutions, serving over 400,000 students across 350+ classroom campuses in 78 cities. Here, the IT and Cybersecurity Leadership Team shares how they standardized on Chrome Enterprise Premium to secure sensitive data and enable zero trust across over 5,000 users. With a workforce that lives in the browser across a SaaS and multi-cloud estate, securing our digital environment is paramount. Our 5,000+ users include faculty, operations, engineering, contractors, and a large Bring Your Own Device (BYOD) population. Operating at this scale, our top priority is protecting student personally identifiable information (PII) flowing through web applications. Under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDPA), protecting this data is critical to regulatory compliance and maintaining brand trust. We needed security within the browser. The challenge of a fragmented browser estate We previously operated a mixed-browser environment, but managing multiple browsers made consistent policy enforcement and visibility challenging. We explored several options to standardize; however, our team didn’t want users to have to learn a new tool, and many of the options had high overhead costs. Testing and rolling out Chrome Enterprise Premium We implemented a phased Chrome Enterprise Premium pilot over a few weeks. Our team first validated the management capabilities in the Google Admin console by testing policy, deployment, extension controls, and reporting. Once we felt confident that Chrome Enterprise Premium provided our desired level of visibility, we rolled it out to several hundred users across various environments, including BYOD, Windows, and macOS. We deployed Safe Browsing and URL filtering for immediate threat protection, DLP rules to restrict copy/paste, downloads, and uploads on sensitive SaaS apps, and context-aware access to restrict application entry based on device posture. The proof of concept succeeded across all criteria including consistent policy enforcement, measurable reduction in risky-site and risky-download events, minimal user friction, and a centralized dashboard to give our teams visibility into managed user activity. The real decision moment came when we realized we could achieve a true Zero Trust posture. With Chrome Enterprise Premium as our backbone, access decisions now happen dynamically based on identity, device posture, and context. A teacher on a school-managed laptop enjoys seamless, full access. On a personal phone, that same educator can review materials without compromising security—downloads and clipboard sharing remain locked down. It delivers airtight data protection without disrupting daily instruction. A simpler, stronger foundation With Chrome Enterprise Premium, we replaced virtual desktops (VDIs) and fragmented security tools with built-in browser protection. Securing the browser itself means we no longer need to install heavy security software on every computer. This makes it easy to apply security policies to personal devices used by contractors and employees. Whether our team uses Windows, macOS, ChromeOS, iOS, or Android, we manage updates, policies, and audit reports from a single Google Admin console. Smart access controls Chrome Enterprise Premium ensures we only grant access when it is safe. Every time someone tries to log in, we verify three things: Identity: Is the user signed into their corporate account? Device: Is the laptop or phone managed and secure? Context: Where are they logging in from, and on what network? Stronger data protection We use Chrome Enterprise’s built-in features, such as Safe Browsing sandboxing and site isolation, and auto-updates to keep end users secure while they work on the web. These benefits plus Chrome Enterprise Premium prove that security does not have to slow down business. Employees work without security interruptions, and our IT team gets a single, clear audit trail across all devices. This helps us maintain high efficiency and supports our regulatory compliance efforts. item.title: Trump talks turkey, and his ballroom, at pardoning event
item.description: President Trump honored a time-worn Washington tradition Tuesday: pardoning poultry — after using the pulpit to praise his White House ballroom and deliver a rally-reminiscent speech. The big picture: Freedom and Feathers, this year's honored birds, continue a bizarre American tradition officially dating back to 1989 — but building on far older presidential lore. Driving the news: "Unfortunately, for 200 years, the White House lacked appropriate accommodations to host such distinguished guests," Trump said at the event, held on the White House's South Lawn. He continued, "I'm pleased to announce that next year we'll be able to have a special location right over there in that rather small ballroom being built." Trump's hotly contested project will be a 90,000-square-foot addition, far larger than the main White House. "I've heard better," he said about the birds' names, though they still earned presidential pardons. Both birds will dodge the oven and retire at Texas A&M University. State of play: The collective 82 pounds of white-feathered flamboyance traveled from West Virginia's Deans Gap Farm for the event. Pointing to his large 2024 election win in West Virginia, Trump said Tuesday, "I won it by a lot. I don't know what the hell happened with this last election. Somebody, please explain it to me." The pair are just four months old. Per a White House fact sheet , Freedom's favorite treat is Dr. Pepper. Feathers prefers to snack on Golden Delicious apples, which — like the turkeys — hail from West Virginia. Between the lines: Trump has never shied away from using the event to ruffle feathers. Last year, he jabbed at former President Biden and attacked Chicago leadership, derailing the focus on his feathered guests by calling Gov. JB Pritzker (D) a "fat slob." During his first term, he joked that the turkeys trotting before him had were slated to "appear in Adam Schiff's basement," a nod to the Democrat who led the 2019 impeachment inquiry into Trump. While Trump has taken presidential rhetoric to a new level, he's not the first to have stuffed political zingers into the bizarre tradition. In 2022, Biden seemingly poked fun at Trump's false claim he'd won the 2020 election, saying : "The votes are in. They've been counted and verified. There's no ballot stuffing. There's no fowl play." Worth noting: PETA called on the White House to end the event, saying presidents are "conned every year into becoming the unpaid spokesperson for factory farmers." President Tracy Reiman called the idea of retirement for the birds "all squawk, no substance, " noting fattened-up turkeys often die prematurely. Flashback: While George H.W. Bush formalized the pardon in 1989, the White House's quirky turkey ties stretch back well over a century. Abraham Lincoln is frequently credited with sparing the first turkey on record at the urging of his son in the 1860s, according to the White House Historical Association. Harry Truman welcomed a live turkey from the National Turkey Federation in 1947, and the photo-op was hatched. item.title: High Stakes in Iraq’s Push to Reclaim Jurf al-Sakhar
item.description: High Stakes in Iraq’s Push to Reclaim Jurf al-Sakhar pfranz Fri, 11/20/2026 - 20:40 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Iraqi soldiers deploy in Jurf al-Sakher, in Babil Province, on November 20, 2026. AHMAD AL-RUBAYE / AFP Q&A / Middle East & North Africa 20 November 2026 8 minutes High Stakes in Iraq’s Push to Reclaim Jurf al-Sakhar On 20 November, Iraqi government forces entered Jurf al-Sakhar, a stronghold of the Iran-backed group Kata’ib Hizbollah. In this Q&A, Crisis Group expert Lahib Higel explains the circumstances that allowed Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi to restore state authority in this area. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Lahib Higel Deputy Program Director, MENA https://twitter.com/LahibHigel Related Tags Iraq What is happening in Jurf al-Sakhar? In mid-November, tensions escalated between Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s government and Kata’ib Hizbollah, an Iran-aligned armed faction, over control of Jurf al-Sakhar, a town on the Euphrates River in Babil governorate about 60km south west of Baghdad. The trigger was an intelligence report alleging that oil has been illegally extracted from pipelines passing through the area and transported to Baghdad for sale. The report suggested that this illicit activity has been taking place since 2021. Zaidi ordered an investigation, and a government committee entered the area on 13 November. It was led by the Hashd al-Shaabi, also known as the Popular Mobilisation Forces, an institution comprising volunteer armed groups that combined to fight ISIS in 2014. The committee also included representatives of the prime minister’s office as well as senior figures from various state bodies. The government subsequently announced that investigators had uncovered evidence of oil smuggling and unauthorised refining, prompting the prime minister to dismiss nine top security and oil sector officials for negligence. His government also publicly accused Kata’ib Hizbollah of involvement in the racket, allegations that the group rejects , claiming the investigation was politically motivated and aimed at compelling it to surrender its weapons. For the prime minister, the episode offered a prized opportunity to restore state control of Jurf al-Sakhar, which has been beyond the reach of successive governments since 2014. He ordered state forces to enter the area and set a 20 November deadline for Kata’ib Hizbollah to withdraw. The government sent reinforcements to Jurf al-Sakhar’s vicinity, and on 19 November the prime minister’s spokesperson issued a statement identifying the forces that were to occupy the area. These included Iraqi army units, federal police, energy police and two Hashd brigades.  Zaidi’s move proved successful. On 20 November, state forces entered Jurf al-Sakhar, following a deal in which Kata’ib Hizbollah agreed to partially withdraw its fighters and redeploy them elsewhere. That said, questions remain regarding the government’s ability to exert its authority over the area and the degree to which Kata’ib Hizbollah will retain influence there through the Hashd, of which it is a member. Why is Jurf al-Sakhar so important? Jurf al-Sakhar is a sub-district of Babil province, bordering Anbar and Baghdad provinces. It sits on an important route leading to Karbala, one of Iraq’s two Shiite shrine cities. The area became an ISIS stronghold in 2014, until state forces and armed groups that mobilised under the Hashd recaptured it in October of that year, displacing thousands of families.  The recapture of Jurf al-Sakhar had huge symbolic weight for Shiite forces, as it was one of the first areas from which they were able to expel ISIS. It also halted the jihadist group’s advance toward Karbala. The Hashd later renamed it Jurf al-Nasr (Victory Cliff), though not everyone enjoyed the fruits of victory: the battle for the area proved devastating to its predominantly Sunni population, which was forced to flee and barred from returning. Twelve years later, some 100,000 of the residents remain displaced . The duration and extent of mass displacement from Jurf al-Sakhar are unique among areas recaptured from ISIS, and the armed groups that took charge in 2014 have never previously turned it back to regular state forces. Jurf al-Sakhar was transformed into a sort of private militarised haven. In recent years, Kata’ib Hizbollah became the main authority there. The area provided the group with a strategic bastion where it maintained a large degree of autonomy. Prior to the fall of the Assad regime in neighbouring Syria, Kata’ib Hizbollah used Jurf al-Sakhar as a conduit for arms transfers from Iran to Syrian forces; the town is also where the group started manufacturing its own weapons, including drones. What drove the government’s confrontation with Kata’ib Hizbollah? The official justification was the investigation into alleged oil smuggling. But the clash stemmed in large part from Zaidi’s bid to strengthen the Iraqi state’s writ and bring armed factions’ independent command structures and weapons under government control. His move to take back the area has a domestic payoff, demonstrating to the Iraqi public that they have a prime minister willing to make highly controversial decisions. Foreign pressure also likely shaped Zaidi’s calculations. Washington has repeatedly urged Baghdad to curb the influence of Iran-aligned armed groups and their economic networks. Since taking office in May, Zaidi has sought to make progress on integrating autonomous armed groups and disarming those that refuse to come under state command. Following the withdrawal of U.S.-led coalition forces on 30 September, he outlined a nine-month disarmament plan. Most armed factions said they were willing to negotiate their status with the government and bring their weapons under central state authority. Two – Kata’ib Hizbollah and Harakat al-Nujaba – resisted. Relations between Zaidi and Kata’ib Hizbollah have been particularly fraught. Relations between Zaidi and Kata’ib Hizbollah have been particularly fraught. The group entered preliminary negotiations with the government, but rejected the prime minister’s plan in October. Tensions rose in early November when Zaidi cancelled service contracts at Mosul airport reportedly linked to armed groups, including Kata’ib Hizbollah, which in turn accused the prime minister and his family of corruption. According to media reports that cited leaked judicial documents, an arrest warrant was issued for the son of Kata’ib Hizbollah’s leader.  The oil smuggling allegations provided Zaidi with the legal justification to take action against the group’s de facto enclave. They also allowed him to attack Kata’ib Hizbollah at its weakest spot, namely the issue of public resources and corruption, rather than that of weapons – a more sensitive matter that the group would almost certainly have resisted from the outset. The prime minister’s overarching goal was not lost on the group’s leaders, but they calculated that it would be hard to challenge Zaidi’s anti-corruption campaign, which several political leaders endorsed at the start of his premiership.  Throughout the dispute with Kata’ib Hizbollah, Zaidi has sought judicial backing for his actions, aiming to portray the fight as a law enforcement matter rather than a political dispute. On 15 November, he met Supreme Judicial Council President Faiq Zaidan to discuss the oil smuggling investigation and possible legal measures against those implicated. Two days later, a judicial investigative committee entered Jurf al-Sakhar to look into any violations and inspect the sites identified in the intelligence report.  Zaidi’s gambit was not without risk, as Kata’ib Hizbollah could have dug in its heels, daring the prime minister to resort to force. Past episodes offer cautionary tales as to the outcome of such armed confrontations. In June 2020, government forces arrested fourteen Kata’ib Hizbollah members suspected of preparing rocket attacks, yet most were released within days following an armed mobilisation against the government. More recently, Zaidi’s own efforts to assert control of armed factions faced resistance, including an unsuccessful attempt to seize weapons from Harakat al-Nujaba in Baghdad in July. Moreover, Kata’ib Hizbollah was well aware that, in the past, Zaidi had made ambitious commitments from which he was forced to backtrack. He first pledged to disarm the groups by 30 September, only to extend the deadline to 30 June 2027 following pushback from hardline factions calling themselves the Islamic Resistance, including Kata’ib Hizbollah and Harakat al-Nujaba. How did Iraq’s Shiite political and armed factions respond? The confrontation exposed differences within the Shia Coordination Framework, the coalition supporting Zaidi’s government. All the Framework leaders were alarmed by the prospect of a battle between the state and the armed groups, fearing it could trigger intra-Shiite strife. Some appeared more open to taking the risk, believing that prior governments had been too cautious vis-à-vis the armed groups. Former Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki – who deployed troops to dismantle the Jaysh al-Mahdi armed group in 2008 – was one of those who seemed amenable to the use of force, at least as a last resort. Others, notably some linked to armed groups that had resisted the U.S. occupation, were more reluctant to threaten the use of force. One such person was Hadi al-Ameri, who heads both the military and political wings of the Badr Organisation. Differences aside, Framework leaders closed ranks in seeking to mediate between Zaidi and Kata’ib Hizbollah, with Ameri, Maliki and Humam Hamoudi, head of the Islamic Supreme Council of Iraq, all playing a part. The three endeavoured to convince Kata’ib Hizbollah to exit the area peacefully, advocating for the group’s gradual withdrawal in conjunction with the deployment of government-aligned forces, including Hashd units not affiliated with Kata’ib Hizbollah.  Kata’ib Hizbollah itself appeared somewhat divided. The group’s competing leadership networks – including those associated with its secretary-general, Abu Hussein al-Hamidawi, and those tied to Abdulaziz al-Mohammadawi, also known as Abu Fadak, who serves as the Hashd chief of staff – disagreed over the idea of withdrawal. Both rejected the government's allegations and maintained that the group needed to retain its weapons independently of the Hashd for the sake of Iraq’s defence. But, according to media reports, Abu Fadak favoured an agreement that would allow government forces alongside Hashd brigades to assume control of parts of Jurf al-Sakhar. In contrast, Hamidawi opposed any concession and allegedly proposed delaying a handover until June 2027, likely believing that Zaidi lacked the political backing to follow through on his threats and that other Shiite leaders would restrain him. Importantly, Iran stepped in to contain the confrontation. Zaidi made a brief, unannounced visit to Tehran on 6 November, during which he met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and parliamentary speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf. His meetings reportedly focused on Iraq’s efforts to mediate between Washington and Tehran, though it came amid growing U.S. pressure on Baghdad to rein in Iran-aligned armed groups. Ten days later, on 16 November, Esmail Qaani, commander of the Revolutionary Guards’ Qods Force, arrived in Iraq for discussions with Shiite politicians and armed factions, including representatives of Kata’ib Hizbollah. His efforts reportedly centred on avoiding a military confrontation between Kata’ib Hizbollah and the Iraqi government, partly by devising an off-ramp that would entail concessions by the group. What does the negotiated settlement look like, and are there risks of escalation? Withdrawal has been partially achieved without a flare-up of violence, which is no small achievement for Zaidi and the mediators. Broadly speaking, the deal entails legal action against those implicated in oil smuggling, Kata’ib Hizbollah’s formal withdrawal from Jurf al-Sakhar and transfer of control of the sub-district to four bodies – the Iraqi army, federal police, counter-terrorism service and Hashd – each of which is responsible for a separate geographic area. In addition, energy police have been deployed to secure oil pipelines in Jurf al-Sakhar.  Questions remain, notably over the scope of Kata’ib Hizbollah’s withdrawal. In particular, it is unclear whether Kata’ib Hizbollah will leave the central area where the 72nd and 79th Hashd brigades have been deployed – or remain there under Hashd cover. Even were Kata’ib Hizbollah to fully withdraw, it is also unclear how the prime minister will view a continued role for the Hashd in the long term. Will he consider the replacement of Kata’ib Hizbollah by other Hashd brigades as an acceptable solution? Or will he see it as essentially redistributing influence over parts of Jurf al-Sakhr without touching the underlying problem of lack of effective government oversight?  The outcome to date is cause for satisfaction in the Iraqi government. But a more sustainable solution, and one more consistent with the government’s agenda, would need to clarify the chain of command, establish full government control of the sub-district and facilitate the return of its displaced residents.  Related Tags More for you Commentary / Middle East & North Africa The U.S.-led Anti-ISIS Coalition is Leaving Iraq: What Happens Next? item.description: by Ifeyinwa Lilian Ezenwosu, John Olajide Olawepo, Jane Nnedinma Ohaekweiro, Peter Ezeogo Ihere, Emeka John Aneke, Justus Uchenna Onu, Oluchukwu Perpetual Okeke, Olajide Odunayo Sobande Introduction Human Papilloma Virus (HPV)-attributable cancers disproportionately affect adolescent girls and young women living with HIV (AGYWLHIV) in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), yet HPV vaccination coverage in this subpopulation remains suboptimal. This systematic review and meta-analysis estimated the pooled prevalence of HPV vaccination coverage among AGYWLHIV in LMICs. Methods A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL), and Web of Science for observational studies published between January 2014 and December 2025. A random-effects meta-analysis was used to estimate the pooled prevalence of HPV vaccination coverage. Subgroup analyses by age group and vaccine type were conducted, while HPV vaccination delivery platforms were summarised descriptively. Publication bias and sensitivity analyses were also performed, and statistical heterogeneity was evaluated using the I² statistic. Results A total of 8 studies involving 1,059 AGYWLHIV were included in the meta-analysis. The pooled HPV vaccination coverage among AGYWLHIV in LMICs was 28.6% (95% CI: 20.3%–38.7%) based on a random-effects model, with substantial heterogeneity across studies (I² = 87.0%, p Conclusion The available evidence from studies conducted in LMICs indicates low HPV vaccination coverage among AGYWLHIV. Integrating HPV vaccination into routine HIV care may represent a potentially useful strategy to improve access and reduce missed vaccination opportunities among AGYWLHIV and should be further evaluated alongside broader efforts supported by strong political commitment and multisectoral collaboration. item.title: From Working Group to SIG Architecture: spotlight on AI Conformance
item.description: In this SIG Architecture spotlight we talked with Janet Kuo (Google) and Yuan Tang (TensorScale AI) about the journey of AI Conformance in Kubernetes, from the initial Working Group to the integration SIG Architecture as a subproject. Introductions Frederico Muñoz and Kirti Goyal (FK): Hi Janet, Yuan, and thank you for the opportunity to learn a bit more about AI Conformance. Can you tell us a bit about yourselves and how you got involved in Kubernetes? Janet Kuo : I'm a Senior Staff Software Engineer at Google and have been a Kubernetes maintainer since 2015, joining the community just as we were racing toward the 1.0 launch. I started my journey writing the core workload controllers that standardized how applications are orchestrated on Kubernetes. Today, I lead SIG Apps as a Co-chair & TL, and also lead the AI Conformance program . My current focus is to ensure Kubernetes remains the best platform for the next generation of workloads, such as AI. Yuan Tang : I'm a co-founder of TensorScale AI where we build AI infrastructure for world models. Prior to that, I was a Senior Principal Software Engineer at Red Hat, where I led the development of Red Hat AI platform and upstream open source strategy. I became involved in Kubernetes early on by fostering collaborations between the Kubernetes community and projects I was leading, including Kubeflow, Argo, and KServe. I later helped found and lead WG Serving and the AI Conformance program, advancing innovation and strengthening community collaboration around running AI workloads on Kubernetes. Program, Working Group, Subproject: the many shapes of AI Conformance FK: AI Conformance started as a CNCF Program, was it then you got involved? Janet Kuo: I was actually involved from day one since I pitched the original idea. It became obvious then that everyone was starting to run AI on Kubernetes, but vendors were building their infrastructure stacks in different ways. I got worried about ecosystem fragmentation. So I wrote up the initial Kubernetes AI Conformance Proposal, took it to the CNCF leadership to get their buy-in, and started the AI Conformance Program. Once we had the green light, I reached out to my fellow co-chairs Yuan Tang, Rita Zhang, and Mario Fahlandt to get the community rallied around it. Yuan Tang: Yes. I was a co-chair of WG Serving at that time and some of the initiatives such as the Gateway AI Inference Extension quickly gained traction. There was a strong interest among the community to include inference-related requirements in the Kubernetes AI Conformance program. FK: How would you describe the motivation behind the creation of the AI Conformance Working Group? Janet and Yuan : The motivation behind creating the Kubernetes AI Conformance Working Group (AI WG) was to address the rapid convergence of AI workloads onto Kubernetes while preventing ecosystem fragmentation. As AI adoption accelerated, organizations began running increasingly complex workloads, including distributed training, large-scale inference, GPU-intensive pipelines, and emerging agentic AI systems across many different Kubernetes platforms. However, vendors were implementing AI infrastructure capabilities differently, especially around GPUs, networking, scheduling, and inference orchestration. That created portability challenges, operational inconsistency, and growing vendor lock-in concerns. The AI WG was formed to bring the community together around: vendor-neutral AI infrastructure standards, interoperable Kubernetes-based AI platforms, consistent operational behavior for AI workloads, and common requirements for scalable AI deployment. FK: WGs are temporary by nature, based on outcomes: would you say the main goals of the WG were achieved? Janet and Yuan : Yes, the WG achieved its primary initial goals. The WG has succeeded in moving the ecosystem from: fragmented, vendor-specific AI infrastructure approaches to a shared, community-defined baseline for AI workloads on Kubernetes. Some concrete indicators of success include: Launching the Certified Kubernetes AI Conformance Program Defining formal Kubernetes AI Requirements (KARs) Getting broad participation from major ecosystem players Growing certified platforms from 18 to 31 within a few months Aligning around newer Kubernetes primitives needed for AI workloads Establishing a roadmap for automated conformance verification Most importantly, the WG created consensus that AI workloads are now a first-class Kubernetes use case. FK: AI Conformance was specifically highlighted at the latest KubeCon: is this a reflection of the growing importance of AI throughout the project? Janet and Yuan : Yes, the prominence of AI Conformance at the latest KubeCon + CloudNativeCon is a strong reflection of how central AI has become to the Kubernetes ecosystem overall. A few years ago, AI workloads on Kubernetes were still viewed as somewhat specialized, mostly tied to ML platforms or GPU-heavy research environments. What’s changed is that AI is now becoming a mainstream infrastructure concern for nearly every large-scale platform operator. That shift naturally elevates AI from an application running on Kubernetes to a core workload category Kubernetes must optimize for. The AI Conformance initiative reflects that evolution. It signals that the community now sees AI infrastructure requirements, things like accelerator scheduling, high-performance networking, workload-aware orchestration, and low-latency inference, as important enough to standardize at the ecosystem level. Its visibility at KubeCon also shows a broader strategic realization: if Kubernetes is going to remain the universal control plane for modern infrastructure, it needs to provide a consistent foundation for AI workloads across clouds, on-prem, and edge environments. So the emphasis on AI Conformance is not just about chasing AI hype; it's about Kubernetes adapting to a major shift in workload patterns and ensuring the ecosystem evolves cohesively rather than fragmenting into vendor-specific AI stacks. From Working Group to SIG Architecture subproject FK: How would you describe the change from WG to SIG? Is it a reflection of AI as something that requires ongoing architectural governance? Janet and Yuan : In Kubernetes, Working Groups are meant to be temporary. Our WG had a specific goal to get the initial Kubernetes AI Conformance requirements published and get the certification process off the ground. Once we hit those milestones, we archived the WG and moved AI Conformance to be a permanent subproject under SIG Architecture. Moving to SIG Architecture definitely proves that AI needs ongoing governance. AI isn’t just a passing trend or a one-off workload. It has become a core part of what Kubernetes runs every day. Because SIG Architecture already owns overall Kubernetes Conformance and API design principles, housing the AI Conformance subproject there makes perfect sense. It makes sure our AI Conformance requirements stay aligned with the rest of the Kubernetes ecosystem for the long haul. FK: And with that change, how would you describe the main goals and areas of intervention of the subproject? Janet and Yuan : Now that we’re a subproject, our main goal is to keep the AI Conformance standards current, vendor-neutral, and standard-setting. We want to make sure Kubernetes captures the latest advancements in AI infrastructure while keeping the ecosystem fair for everyone. When we find gaps where no clear community pattern exists, we help foster and form new standards to solve them. AI Conformance and Kubernetes FK: AI Infrastructure is evolving very quickly, while Kubernetes APIs are designed to remain stable for years. Is this something you consider a challenge? Janet and Yuan : It’s definitely a tricky balance. AI moves very fast, while Kubernetes is designed to be stable and boring. But we actually structured the program around this exact tension. First, we use a tiered graduation model. When new AI infrastructure concepts emerge, we introduce them as recommended SHOULD requirements. That gives the ecosystem room to experiment and agree on best practices without locking Kubernetes into rigid APIs too early. Once those APIs stabilize and with ecosystem adoption, we graduate them to mandatory MUST requirements. Second, we intentionally keep our focus on the infrastructure layer. We test for core capabilities like accelerator support through Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA), rather than getting bogged down in specific AI frameworks or model servers. That keeps the base platform stable while letting the AI tooling evolve as fast as it needs to. FK: DRA has evolved, also due to the work of WG Device Management, as an important part of Kubernetes (and especially so for AI workloads), with SIG Architecture having an important role in how it’s integrated in Kubernetes: do you find any parallel in this? Specifically, do you think there will be a heavier focus in the integration with the evolving Kubernetes architecture as part of SIG Architecture? Janet and Yuan : There is a huge parallel there. Whenever we face a massive, complicated challenge that touches multiple parts of the codebase and involves multiple SIGs, a Working Group is the best place to start. It lets experts from different SIGs get together to figure out the problem, and build consensus. Being part of SIG Architecture means there will be a much heavier focus on how AI capabilities weave into the evolving Kubernetes architecture. Instead of treating AI as an add-on layer, we’re looking at how core Kubernetes primitives, like scheduling and resource allocation, need to adapt at a foundational level to support the next decade of AI workloads. Final remarks FK: For interested contributors, what’s the best way to get involved with the AI Conformance subproject? Janet and Yuan : We're always looking for new contributors. The easiest way to get started is by checking out our main repo at kubernetes-sigs/ai-conformance and join our meetings . If you're interested in defining new AI Conformance requirements, you can jump into PR reviews or propose your own using our KAR template . If you want to write code, we always need help expanding our automated Go test suites in the test/ directory . For vendors looking to certify their platforms, all the details are at cncf/k8s-ai-conformance . FK: Any final comments you would like to share? Janet and Yuan : We’ve been blown away by how fast the community has rallied around this. When we first announced the AI Conformance program during the keynote at KubeCon NA 2025 , we weren’t sure what the response would be. But by the time we gave our update keynote at KubeCon EU 2026 , we had grown from 18 certified platforms to 31 in just a few months. That kind of growth shows just how much the industry wanted a unified, vendor-neutral standard. It gives organizations the confidence that they can run their AI workloads on any certification Kubernetes platform without getting locked into a proprietary stack. If you’re a platform vendor, we’d love to see you get certified. If you’re a developer interested in the intersection of AI and cloud-native infrastructure, come join us in SIG Architecture! FK: Excellent, thank you both for guiding us in this journey on AI and AI Conformance in Kubernetes.

item.title: Harness Engineering for Self-Improvement
item.description: The concept of recursive self-improvement (RSI) dates back to I. J. Good (1965) , where he defined an “ultraintelligent machine” as a system that can surpass humans in all intellectual activities and design better machines to improve itself. Yudkowsky (2008) used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” for a specific feedback loop: an AI uses its current intelligence to improve the cognitive machinery that produces its intelligence. This feedback loop in modern AI may indicate the model rewriting its own weights directly, or more broadly the model improves the training pipeline and the deployment system , which in turn enables a better successor model with improved performance across economically valuable tasks. The speed of research development in AI has been shown to drastically accelerated in frontier labs ( Anthropic ; OpenAI ).

item.title: Common pitfalls when building generative AI applications
item.description: As we’re still in the early days of building applications with foundation models, it’s normal to make mistakes. This is a quick note with examples of some of the most common pitfalls that I’ve seen, both from public case studies and from my personal experience. Because these pitfalls are common, if you’ve worked on any AI product, you’ve probably seen them before. 1. Use generative AI when you don't need generative AI Every time there’s a new technology, I can hear the collective sigh of senior engineers everywhere: “Not everything is a nail.” Generative AI isn’t an exception — its seemingly limitless capabilities only exacerbate the tendency to use generative AI for everything. A team pitched me the idea of using generative AI to optimize energy consumption. They fed a household’s list of energy-intensive activities and hourly electricity prices into an LLM, then asked it to create a schedule to minimize energy costs. Their experiments showed that this could help reduce a household’s electricity bill by 30%. Free money. Why wouldn’t anyone want to use their app? I asked: “How does it compare to simply scheduling the most energy-intensive activities when electricity is cheapest? Say, doing your laundry and charging your car after 10pm?” They said they would try it later and let me know. They never followed up, but they abandoned this app soon after. I suspect that this greedy scheduling can be quite effective. Even if it’s not, there are other much cheaper and more reliable optimization solutions than generative AI, like linear programming. I’ve seen this scenario over and over again. A big company wants to use generative AI to detect anomalies in network traffic. Another wants to predict upcoming customer call volume. A hospital wants to detect whether a patient is malnourished (really not recommended). It can often be beneficial to explore a new approach to get a sense of what’s possible, as long as you’re aware that your goal isn’t to solve a problem but to test a solution. “We solve the problem” and “We use generative AI” are two very different headlines, and unfortunately, so many people would rather have the latter. 2. Confuse 'bad product' with 'bad AI' At the other end of the spectrum, many teams dismiss gen AI as a valid solution for their problems because they tried it out and their users hated it. However, other teams successfully used gen AI for similar use cases. I could only look into two of these teams. In both cases, the issue wasn’t with AI, but with product. Many people have told me that the technical aspects of their AI applications are straightforward. The hard part is user experience (UX). What should the product interface look like? How to seamlessly integrate the product into the user workflow? How to incorporate human-in-the-loop? UX has always been challenging, but it’s even more so with generative AI. While we know that generative AI is changing how we read, write, learn, teach, work, entertain, etc., we don’t quite know how yet. What will the future of reading/learning/working be like? Here are some simple examples to show how what users want can be counter-intuitive and need rigorous user study. My friend works on an application that summarizes meeting transcripts. Initially, her team focused on getting the right summary length. Would users prefer 3-sentence summaries or 5-sentence summaries? However, it turned out that their users didn’t care about the actual summary. They only wanted action items specific to them from each meeting. When LinkedIn developed a chatbot for skill fit assessment, they discovered that users didn’t want correct responses. Users wanted helpful responses. For example, if a user asks a bot whether they’re a fit for a job and the bot responds with: “You’re a terrible fit,” this response might be correct but not very helpful to the user. Users want tips on what the gaps are and what they can do to close the gaps. Intuit built a chatbot to help users answer tax questions. Initially, they got lukewarm feedback — users didn’t find the bot useful. After investigation, they found out that users actually hated typing. Facing a blank chatbot, users didn’t know what the bot could do and what to type. So, for each interaction, Intuit added a few suggested questions for users to click on. This reduced the friction for users to use the bot and gradually built users’ trust. The feedback from users then became much more positive. (Shared by Nhung Ho , VP of AI at Intuit, during our panel at Grace Hopper.) Because everyone uses the same models nowadays, the AI components of AI products are similar, and the differentiation is product. 3. Start too complex Examples of this pitfall: Use an agentic framework when direct API calls work. Agonize over what vector database to use when a simple term-based retrieval solution (that doesn’t require a vectordb) works. Insist on finetuning when prompting works. Use semantic caching. Given so many shiny new technologies, it’s tempting to jump straight into using them. However, incorporating external tools too early can cause 2 problems: Abstract away critical details, making it hard to understand and debug your system. Introduce unnecessary bugs. Tool developers can make mistakes. For example, I often find typos in default prompts when reviewing a framework’s codebase. If the framework you use updates its prompt without telling you, your application’s behaviors might change and you might not know why. Eventually, abstractions are good. But abstractions need to incorporate best practices and be tested overtime. As we’re still in the early days of AI engineering, best practices are still evolving, we should be more vigilant when adopting any abstraction. 4. Over-index on early success It took LinkedIn 1 month to achieve 80% of the experience they wanted, and an additional 4 months to surpass 95% . The initial success made them grossly underestimate how challenging it is to improve the product, especially around hallucinations. They found it discouraging how difficult it was to achieve each subsequent 1% gain. A startup that develops AI sales assistants for ecommerce told me that getting from 0 to 80% took as long as from 80% to 90% . The challenges they faced: Accuracy/latency tradeoff: more planning/self-correction = more nodes = higher latency Tool calling: hard for agents to differentiate similar tools Hard for tonal requests (e.g. "talk like a luxury brand concierge" ) in the system prompt to be perfectly obeyed Hard for the agent to completely understand customers’ intent Hard to create a specific set of unit tests because the combination of queries is basically infinite Thanks Jason Tjahjono for sharing this. In the paper UltraChat, Ding et al. (2023) shared that “ the journey from 0 to 60 is easy, whereas progressing from 60 to 100 becomes exceedingly challenging .” This is perhaps one of the first painful lessons anyone who has built an AI product quickly learns. It’s easy to build a demo, but hard to build a product. Other than the issues of hallucinations, latency, latency/accuracy tradeoff, tool use, prompting, testing, … as mentioned, teams also run into issues, such as: Reliability from the API providers. A team told me that 10% of their API calls timed out. Or product’s behaviors change because the underlying model changes. Compliance , e.g. around AI output copyrights, data access/sharing, user privacy, security risks from retrieval/caching systems, and ambiguity around training data lineage. Safety , e.g. bad actors abusing your product, your product generates insensitive or offensive responses. When planning a product’s milestones and resources, make sure to take into account these potential roadblocks. A friend calls this “being cautiously optimistic”. However, remember that many cool demos don’t lead to wonderful products. 5. Forgo human evaluation To automatically evaluate AI applications, many teams opt for the AI-as-a-judge (also called LLM-as-a-judge) approach — using AI models to evaluate AI outputs. A common pitfall is forgoing human evaluation to rely entirely on AI judges. While AI judges can be very useful, they aren’t deterministic. The quality of a judge depends on the underlying judge’s model, the judge’s prompt, and the use case. If the AI judge isn’t developed properly, it can give misleading evaluations about your application’s performance. AI judges must be evaluated and iterated over time, just like all other AI applications. The teams with the best products I’ve seen all have human evaluation to supplement their automated evaluation. Every day, they have human experts evaluate a subset of their application’s outputs, which can be anywhere from 30 - 1000 examples. Daily manual evaluation serves 3 purposes: Correlate human judgments with AI judgments. If the score by human evaluators is decreasing but the score by AI judges is increasing, you might want to investigate your AI judges. Gain a better understanding of how users use your application, which can give you ideas to improve your application. Detect patterns and changes in users’ behaviors, using your knowledge of current events, that automated data exploration might miss. The reliability of human evaluation also depends on well-crafted annotation guidelines. These annotation guidelines can help improve the model’s instructions (if a human has a hard time following the instructions, the model will, too). It can also be reused to create finetuning data later if you choose to finetune. In every project I’ve worked on, staring at data for just 15 minutes usually gives me some insight that could save me hours of headaches . Greg Brockman tweeted: “ Manual inspection of data has probably the highest value-to-prestige ratio of any activity in machine learning. ” 6. Crowdsource use cases This is a mistake I saw in the early days when enterprises were in a frenzy to adopt generative AI. Unable to come up with a strategy for what use cases to focus on, many tech executives crowdsourced ideas from the whole company. “We hire smart people. Let them tell us what to do.” They then try to implement these ideas one by one. And that’s how we ended up with a million text-to-SQL models, a million Slack bots, and a billion code plugins. While it’s indeed a good idea to listen to the smart people that you hire, individuals might be biased toward the problems that immediately affect their day-to-day work instead of problems that might bring the highest returns on investment. Without an overall strategy that considers the big picture, it’s easy to get sidetracked into a series of small, low-impact applications and come to the wrong conclusion that gen AI has no ROI. Summary In short, here are the common AI engineering pitfalls: Use generative AI when you don’t need generative AI Gen AI isn’t a one-size-fits-all solution to all problems. Many problems don’t even need AI. Confuse ‘bad product’ with ‘bad AI’ For many AI product, AI is the easy part, product is the hard part. Start too complex While fancy new frameworks and finetuning can be useful for many projects, they shouldn’t be your first course of action. Over-index on early success Initial success can be misleading. Going from demo-ready to production-ready can take much longer than getting to the first demo. Forgo human evaluation AI judges should be validated and correlated with systematic human evaluation. Crowdsource use cases Have a big-picture strategy to maximize return on investment.
